paragraphs.context: Many years ago, I journeyed overland from Greece to Nepal.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer remembers a trip through the desert.
paragraphs.simple: Many years ago the writer traveled by land from Greece to Nepal. She rode in a van through the desert from Damascus in Syria to Baghdad in Iraq. At sunset she found a tea tent in the middle of nowhere. An old man and his great-grandson gave her tea and dinner and let her camp there. She never forgot their kindness, the beautiful sunset and the cold starry night. Writing this book let her remember that trip.
paragraphs.tone: Warm and thankful, like a letter to a friend.

background.note: Damascus is the capital of Syria, a country in the Middle East. It is one of the oldest cities in the world.
Baghdad is the capital of Iraq, a country in the Middle East. About 1,200 years ago it was one of the biggest and richest cities in the world.
Nepal is a small country in the Himalaya mountains, between China and India.

paragraphs.context: One summer day, a mysterious tree house appeared in the woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: How the tree house story began.
paragraphs.simple: One summer a magic tree house appeared in the woods. It can take Jack and Annie to any time and place. It belongs to Morgan le Fay, a magic librarian from Camelot.

background.note: Morgan le Fay is a magic librarian from the King Arthur stories. The tree house belongs to her.
Camelot is the castle and city of King Arthur in the old stories. Merlin and Morgan live there.

paragraphs.context: After Jack and Annie traveled on many adventures for Morgan
paragraphs.simple: Later, Merlin began to send them on "Merlin Missions". With help from Teddy and Kathleen, two young sorcerers, they went to four places from old stories and found things to help save Camelot.

background.note: Merlin is a famous wizard in the old stories about King Arthur. In the "Merlin Missions" books, Merlin sends Jack and Annie on special jobs.
Teddy is a young sorcerer and Kathleen is a "selkie" (a seal girl) from earlier Merlin Missions. Both are learning magic from Morgan.

paragraphs.context: On their next four Merlin Missions, Jack and Annie were told
paragraphs.simple: Now they must go to real places in history and show Merlin that they can use magic wisely. They have just come back from Venice, 250 years ago, and they are waiting for Merlin again.

background.note: In the last book, "Carnival at Candlelight", Jack and Annie went to Venice, Italy, in the 1740s and saved the city from a flood.

paragraphs.context: Jack put his math homework aside.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack looks at the book of magic rhymes again.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stops doing his math homework. He takes a small handmade book out of his drawer and looks at its title again, as he has done many times.

paragraphs.context: For weeks, Jack had kept the book hidden in his drawer
paragraphs.mainIdea: The rules of the magic book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has hidden the book for weeks. It has ten magic rhymes for four missions, and each rhyme works only once. They already used two in Venice.

paragraphs.context: “Jack!” Annie rushed into Jack’s room.
paragraphs.simple: Annie runs into Jack's room with shining eyes and tells him to bring the book.

paragraphs.context: Jack quickly put Teddy and Kathleen’s book into his backpack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the book in his backpack, puts on his jacket and runs downstairs.

paragraphs.context: “Because I just saw it!” Annie shouted.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie has seen the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she has just seen the tree house. She hurries across the yard.

paragraphs.context: “Just now!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was walking home from the library when she had a feeling. She went to look, and the tree house was there.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie raced into the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They run to the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: They run into the woods. It is early spring: the trees have new buds and the moss is green. They come to the tallest oak tree.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up town in Pennsylvania, USA, where Jack and Annie live.

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” breathed Jack. He stared up at the magic tree house.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They climb into the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looks up at the tree house. The rope ladder hangs down. They climb up, and Jack takes off his backpack.

paragraphs.context: “Look, a book and a letter!” Annie said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find a letter and a book.
paragraphs.simple: Annie picks up a folded letter, and Jack picks up a book with a gold cover.

paragraphs.context: “A golden age?” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to go at once.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks "a golden age" sounds great and wants to go.

background.note: A "golden age" is a time when a place or people are at their best: rich, peaceful, and making great art and science. Baghdad's golden age was about 1,200 years ago.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Annie. She unfolded the paper.
paragraphs.simple: Annie opens the letter. It is in Merlin's handwriting, and she reads it aloud.

paragraphs.context: Dear Jack and Annie of Frog Creek,
paragraphs.simple: Merlin says their job is to go to Baghdad long ago and help the caliph spread wisdom to the world. They must be humble and use their magic wisely.

paragraphs.context: “Wait, what’s a caliph?” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not know what a caliph is. He also thinks "spread wisdom to the world" is a very big job.

background.note: A caliph was a ruler of the Muslim world, both a king and a religious leader. In Baghdad's golden age, the caliph ruled a huge empire.

paragraphs.context: Follow these instructions:
paragraphs.simple: They must ride "a ship of the desert" on a cold night full of stars, and then ride through dust and hot morning light.

paragraphs.context: Find a horse on a dome,
paragraphs.simple: They must find a horse on top of a dome, "the one who sees all". It is in the center of the city, behind the third wall.

paragraphs.context: Beneath birds who sing
paragraphs.simple: Under singing birds, in the Room of the Tree, they will meet an old friend and a new friend.

paragraphs.context: Remember that life
paragraphs.simple: Life has many surprises. They must go back to the tree house before the moon comes up.

paragraphs.context: “No, it doesn’t,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks it is not easy.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the instructions are very mysterious. They do not understand any of them.

paragraphs.context: “We’ll find out when we get there,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie tells Jack to make the wish.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they will understand when they get there. First Jack must make the wish.

paragraphs.context: “Okay,” said Jack. He pointed to the cover of the book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack points to the book and wishes to go to the golden age of Baghdad.

paragraphs.context: The wind started to blow.
paragraphs.simple: The wind begins to blow.

paragraphs.context: Then everything was still.
paragraphs.simple: Then everything stops moving. It is completely quiet.

paragraphs.context: Jack felt hot. He opened his eyes.
paragraphs.simple: It is very hot. Sunlight floods into the tree house. Jack and Annie now wear long robes, white head cloths and pointed shoes. Jack's backpack is now a leather bag.

paragraphs.context: “We look like characters in that book Aunt Mary gave us,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They look like people from old stories.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they look like people in "Tales from the Arabian Nights", a book their aunt gave them.

background.note: "The Arabian Nights" (also "One Thousand and One Nights") is a very old collection of stories from the Middle East. Some stories happen in Baghdad.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, like Aladdin and Ali Baba,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they look like Aladdin and Ali Baba.

background.note: Aladdin (with his magic lamp) and Ali Baba (with the forty thieves) are two famous heroes of the Arabian Nights stories.

paragraphs.context: Shading their eyes from the bright sunlight
paragraphs.simple: The tree house is at the top of the tallest palm tree in a small group of palm trees. There are bushes, a little grass and a small spring of water. All around are miles of very hot sand.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah, and where’s Baghdad?” asked Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks where Baghdad is and starts to read their research book.

paragraphs.context: From 762 AD to 1258 AD, the Arab world had a golden age.
paragraphs.simple: From the year 762 to 1258, the Arab world had a golden age. A ruler called a caliph ruled a huge empire. Its capital was Baghdad, a center for learning and trade.

background.note: After the 600s, Arab rulers built a very large empire, from Spain in the west to central Asia in the east.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. “So the caliph is a ruler,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack understands that the caliph is a ruler who probably lived in Baghdad.

paragraphs.context: “Patience,” said Jack. “Remember
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie to be patient. On their last trip they learned to do things in order, one at a time. He reads Merlin's first instruction again.

paragraphs.context: “Well, whatever it is, I’m sure we’ll find it eventually,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they will find it in the end. They could sit and watch for a big boat... or do something else.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: Annie is not really patient.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe we could use one of Teddy and Kathleen’s magic rhymes.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to use a rhyme.
paragraphs.simple: Annie wants to use one of the magic rhymes.

paragraphs.context: “Not yet,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must use magic wisely. They have just arrived, and they have only eight rhymes left for three missions.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, okay—” Annie broke in.
paragraphs.simple: Annie agrees: they can only use a rhyme when there is nothing else they can do.

paragraphs.context: “Walk where?” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They do not know the way.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks which way Baghdad is.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked out the window. Beyond the palm trees
paragraphs.simple: Outside there is only sand and sky, with lonely sand hills far away. The desert is strangely quiet.

paragraphs.context: “We could, uh …” Jack couldn’t think of anything else
paragraphs.mainIdea: They look at the rhyme book.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot think of anything else, so they look at the list of rhymes in the book.

paragraphs.context: “Make a Stone Come Alive,” read Annie.
paragraphs.simple: They used "Make a Stone Come Alive" in Venice, so they cannot use it again.

paragraphs.context: “It wouldn’t help, anyway,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: "Bend Iron" is used too. Annie reads "Turn into Ducks", but Jack says no.

paragraphs.context: “Mend What Cannot Be Mended,” read Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie reads "Mend What Cannot Be Mended", but nothing is broken.

paragraphs.context: “How about this one?” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie finds "Make Helpers Appear out of Nowhere".

paragraphs.context: “Come on, it’s perfect,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it is perfect: they are in "nowhere", and they really need helpers.
paragraphs.tone: Funny: a play on the word "nowhere".

paragraphs.context: “Okay,” said Jack. “I’ll read the line Teddy wrote.
paragraphs.simple: Jack will read Teddy's line, and Annie will read Kathleen's line in her selkie language.

background.note: In old Scottish and Irish stories, selkies are seals that can become people. Kathleen is a selkie.

paragraphs.context: The second that Annie finished the rhyme
paragraphs.simple: As soon as Annie finishes, wind blows sand into the tree house. The palm trees shake, and sand gets in Annie's eyes.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie jumped away from the window.
paragraphs.simple: They stand against the wall and cover their faces. Sand keeps blowing in.

paragraphs.context: The hot sand piled into drifts all over the floor.
paragraphs.simple: Hot sand makes small hills on the floor. Then the wind stops as fast as it started.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie looked out the window. The air was thick
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dust is still in the air.
paragraphs.simple: The air is full of dust and hard to see through, but the sand is not moving now.

paragraphs.context: “I hope so,” said Jack. “Why did our magic rhyme cause a sandstorm
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks why the rhyme made a sandstorm, not helpers. Annie thinks maybe they said it wrong.

paragraphs.context: Jack brushed the sand off their research book
paragraphs.simple: Jack cleans the book and finds "sandstorms" in the index.

paragraphs.context: The season of the sandstorms begins in the desert in mid-February
paragraphs.simple: Sandstorms start in the middle of February and go on all spring. The wind can blow 40 miles (about 65 km) an hour. Travelers can easily get lost.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t understand,” said Jack. “We don’t need to lose our way.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they do not need to get lost; they need to find their way.

paragraphs.context: Just then the sound of bells came from outside.
paragraphs.simple: Just then they hear bells outside.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie looked out the window. Through the haze
paragraphs.simple: Through the dusty air they see four riders high on camels, in bright robes. Behind them are twelve more camels tied in a line and carrying heavy bags. Bells ring on the camels' necks.

paragraphs.context: Annie grinned. “Helpers!” she said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie smiles: the rhyme worked. Here are the helpers!

paragraphs.context: Annie stuck her head out the tree house window.
paragraphs.simple: Annie calls to the riders. Jack pulls her back: it is too hard to explain the tree house, so they should go down first.

paragraphs.context: “Good point,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie gives Jack the letter and climbs down. Jack puts the letter and both books in his bag and follows her.

paragraphs.context: When he stepped onto the ground, Jack twisted the rope ladder
paragraphs.simple: Jack hides the rope ladder behind the tree so no one will see it.

paragraphs.context: The camel riders headed toward the palm trees.
paragraphs.simple: The leader makes his camel kneel and gets off. He has a black beard and serious dark eyes. He does not smile and asks who they are.

paragraphs.context: “I am Annie, and this is my brother, Jack,”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says their home is far away in Frog Creek, Pennsylvania.

paragraphs.context: “I have not heard of such a place,” the man said.
paragraphs.simple: The man has never heard of that place. He asks why they are alone in the desert.

paragraphs.context: “We were riding with our family,” Annie said.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they were traveling with their big family, fell asleep behind the trees, and were left behind by mistake.

paragraphs.context: The man looked concerned. “Why have they not come back for you?”
paragraphs.simple: The man looks worried. He hopes robbers (bandits) have not attacked their family.

paragraphs.context: “There are many bandits prowling the desert,” said the man.
paragraphs.simple: The man says many bandits move around the desert. Jack looks nervously at the huge sandy land.

paragraphs.context: “That is why one must always travel with others,”
paragraphs.simple: The man says people must always travel in groups. He hopes their family will come back soon.

paragraphs.context: “Excuse me,” Annie said politely. “But who are you?
paragraphs.simple: Annie politely asks who he is and why he came here.

paragraphs.context: “I am a merchant,” the man said.
paragraphs.simple: He is a merchant. His caravan came from the west, and a sudden sandstorm brought them to this oasis. They will rest and give the animals water, and travel to Baghdad in the cool night.

background.note: A caravan is a group of merchants (traders) traveling together with camels across the desert, carrying things to sell.
A small green place in a desert where there is water and trees can grow.

paragraphs.context: The caravan leader walked over to his men
paragraphs.simple: The leader talks to his men. They get off and take the bags off the camels.

paragraphs.context: Annie turned to Jack. “See, our rhyme worked!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie whispers that the rhyme worked: the magic sandstorm brought helpers who are going to Baghdad.

paragraphs.context: “Well, Merlin said we should be humble
paragraphs.simple: Merlin said they should be humble, so Annie decides to offer help. The leader is getting water from the spring.

paragraphs.context: The man gave her a quick smile.
paragraphs.simple: The man smiles and asks them to gather dates for his hungry men. He gives Annie two baskets.

paragraphs.context: Annie carried the baskets to Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie does not know what a date is.

paragraphs.context: “I’ll look it up,” said Jack. With his back
paragraphs.simple: Jack hides the book from the riders and looks up "dates".

paragraphs.context: Dates are known as the fruit of the desert.
paragraphs.simple: Dates are "the fruit of the desert". They hang in bunches from date palms. People shake the tree to get them. The wood and leaves of the tree are useful too.

background.note: The date palm is a tall palm tree that grows in hot, dry places like the Middle East. People have eaten its sweet fruit for thousands of years.

paragraphs.context: “Okay, got it,” interrupted Annie
paragraphs.simple: Annie stops Jack's reading: she wants to start shaking trees.

paragraphs.context: Jack put the book away and looked around.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees the brown fruit in the trees. They shake a tree together until dates fall.

paragraphs.context: In the desert heat, Jack and Annie went from tree to tree
paragraphs.simple: They shake tree after tree in the heat. When their baskets are full, the shadows are long: it is late afternoon.

paragraphs.context: Tired and sweaty, Jack and Annie carried their heavy baskets
paragraphs.simple: They take the heavy baskets to the leader, who is boiling water on a small fire. He thanks them.

paragraphs.context: “You should rest from the heat now,” said the man.
paragraphs.simple: The man tells them to rest and invites them to have tea.

paragraphs.context: “My name is very long,” the man said with a smile.
paragraphs.simple: He says his name is long, so they can call him Mamoon.

background.note: Abdullah al-Mamoon (also spelled al-Ma'mun) was a real caliph of Baghdad (ruled 813-833). He loved books and science.

paragraphs.context: While their camels grazed, Mamoon and his men sat
paragraphs.simple: They sit on a wool rug and share dates and tea. The dates are sweet and soft; the tea is strong but good.

paragraphs.context: In the fiery red glow of the setting sun, Jack watched
paragraphs.simple: At sunset Jack watches the camels. They look funny: knobby knees, big feet, small moving ears and big lips. Some eat whole thorny branches without chewing.

paragraphs.context: “No,” said the caravan leader. “Their mouths are very tough.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says camels have very tough mouths and can eat anything: sticks and bones. A young rider jokes that they even eat tents and bags.

paragraphs.context: “Our bags are filled with goods from Greece, Turkey, and Syria,”
paragraphs.simple: Their bags have jewels, beads and costly spices like cinnamon, pepper and vanilla from Greece, Turkey and Syria. They will sell them in Baghdad.

background.note: In the Middle Ages, spices like pepper and cinnamon came from far away and cost a lot. Merchants became rich by trading them.

paragraphs.context: “We have to meet with the caliph.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they have to meet the caliph.

paragraphs.context: The camel riders chuckled as if they thought Annie was making a joke.
paragraphs.simple: The riders laugh because they think Annie is joking.

paragraphs.context: Only Mamoon did not laugh.
paragraphs.simple: Only Mamoon does not laugh. He asks if their family will meet the caliph.

paragraphs.context: “No,” said Annie. “Just Jack and me.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she and Jack will help the caliph spread wisdom. Jack warns her to stop.

paragraphs.context: “The caliph does not meet with children,” said a young man.
paragraphs.simple: A young man says the caliph does not meet children; he is the most powerful person in the world.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon looked at Annie and Jack with a curious expression.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon looks at them with interest. It will soon be night. He asks them to travel with the caravan to Baghdad on camels.

paragraphs.context: “Sure we can!” said Annie. “We love camels!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they love camels. Jack is not so sure.

paragraphs.context: “Good. We love our ships of the desert, too,” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Ships of the desert are camels.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon calls camels "ships of the desert" and says they will "set sail" soon. Now Annie understands Merlin's words.

paragraphs.context: Camels, thought Jack. Oh, brother.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks: we have to ride camels. Oh, no!

paragraphs.context: The camel riders all silently watched the sun set
paragraphs.simple: The riders quietly watch the sun go down behind the sand hills. The desert turns red. When the sun is gone, the air gets much colder.

paragraphs.context: The camel riders put out their small fire.
paragraphs.simple: The riders put out the fire, put saddles on the camels and load the bags.

paragraphs.context: Then Mamoon came over to Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon gives them two camel sisters to ride. They should come to the front of the line and ride with him.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie walked over to the two camel sisters.
paragraphs.simple: Each camel has reins on her neck and a pile of colorful cushions on her hump as a saddle.

paragraphs.context: Annie patted the wiry, tan-colored fur of one of the camels.
paragraphs.simple: Annie pets one camel, which moves its long eyelashes at her. She calls it "Cutie" and the other one "Beauty".

paragraphs.context: “Cutie and Beauty?” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not think either camel is cute or beautiful.

paragraphs.context: Cutie rose awkwardly up from a kneeling position
paragraphs.simple: Cutie stands up clumsily. Annie is now very high above Jack.

paragraphs.context: Jack started to climb onto Beauty.
paragraphs.simple: When Jack starts to climb on, Beauty chews the end of his head cloth.

paragraphs.context: “Stop that!” said Jack, pulling the cloth away from her.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pulls the cloth away. Beauty opens her mouth and shows sharp teeth, and Jack moves back.

paragraphs.context: “Easy for you to say,” said Jack. “Yours likes you.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it is easy for Annie; her camel likes her.

paragraphs.context: “Don’t worry, Beauty likes you, too,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says Beauty likes Jack too. Her camel walks toward the others, ready to leave.

paragraphs.context: “Fun,” muttered Jack. “Right.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not believe it will be fun. He gets onto Beauty's hump. She looks at him and hits his back with her tail.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried to get comfortable on the saddle cushion.
paragraphs.simple: Beauty spits at Jack and makes a strange high noise.

paragraphs.context: “Quiet!” said Jack. He hooked his shoulder bag
paragraphs.simple: Jack hangs his bag on the saddle. Then Beauty turns and chews the bag.

paragraphs.context: “No! Don’t!” yelled Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Beauty pull the bag in two directions. Jack calls her stupid.

paragraphs.context: Jack jumped. Mamoon had ridden up behind him
paragraphs.simple: Jack is surprised: Mamoon is behind him, watching.

paragraphs.context: Jack was embarrassed. “Um,
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels embarrassed. He says the camel will not let go of his things.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon grabbed the strap of Jack’s bag.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon makes a sound with his tongue and the camel lets go. He hangs the bag on the saddle again.

paragraphs.context: “For thousands of years, camels like this one
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says camels have carried people across the desert for thousands of years. A camel is a wonder of nature.

background.note: Camels are well made for deserts. They store fat (not water) in their humps, and they can close their noses against blowing sand.

paragraphs.context: “She can drink two barrels of water in ten minutes,”
paragraphs.simple: A camel can drink two barrels of water in ten minutes, then go a week without drinking. She can go many days without food.

paragraphs.context: “She is well suited to travel in the desert,”
paragraphs.simple: Her thick eyebrows protect her eyes from the strong sun. Her long eyelashes and ear fur keep the sand out.

paragraphs.context: “Her feet are so tough, they do not feel the heat
paragraphs.simple: Her tough feet do not feel the hot sand. Her big feet stop her from sinking into soft sand.

paragraphs.context: “She can carry five hundred pounds of baggage
paragraphs.simple: She can carry 500 pounds (about 230 kg) and travel 100 miles (160 km) in one day.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon tugged on the camel’s reins
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon pulls the reins and clucks. Beauty stands up on her long, strong legs.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon looked at Jack. “We must respect her and honor her,”
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says they must respect the camel. In many ways she is better than people.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded. He thought of the words of Merlin’s letter.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers that Merlin said they must be humble. He pats the camel kindly.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon clucked his tongue again to coax the camel forward.
paragraphs.simple: Beauty walks forward. Jack rocks from side to side high up. He does not feel safe, but he stays calm.

paragraphs.context: The desert sky was bright with stars.
paragraphs.simple: The sky is full of stars, and the caravan starts to move.

paragraphs.context: The camels walked with a swaying motion.
paragraphs.simple: Camels move both legs on one side, then both legs on the other side, so they rock from left to right, like a ship.

paragraphs.context: “Sort of,” said Jack, shivering.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is not having fun. He feels sick and cold. He worries: will the caliph meet them, how can they spread wisdom, and how will they find the tree house again?

paragraphs.context: Mamoon slowed his camel until he was riding between Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says when he was a boy, he rode with his father on cold desert trips. At first he also thought camels were silly and wanted his warm bed at home.

paragraphs.context: “But over time, I have come to love the cold desert nights,”
paragraphs.simple: Little by little Mamoon came to love desert nights. Now, at home, he wants to be in the desert reading the wind and the stars.

paragraphs.context: “They have their own language,” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: The stars have their own language. Now they are going east, toward the Goat Star.

background.note: The Goat Star is the bright star Capella. Its name means "little she-goat". Desert travelers used stars like it to find their way at night.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t tell which star was the Goat Star.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot find the Goat Star, but he is amazed. There are more stars than he ever imagined, and some look close enough to touch.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon started singing a song.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon sings and the others join in. Jack does not know the words, but the music is calming.

paragraphs.context: Jack stopped worrying about how they would get back
paragraphs.simple: Jack stops worrying and starts to enjoy the fresh air.

paragraphs.context: “Jack,” Annie said softly. “Guess what
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they have done the first part of Merlin's letter: riding a ship of the desert on a cold starry night.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly a fierce shout came from the distance.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly someone shouts far away. Jack's heart beats fast. A camel driver shouts "Bandits!"

paragraphs.context: Jack looked around wildly.
paragraphs.simple: Dark men on horses are riding fast across the sand toward them, shouting.

paragraphs.context: “We will fight them off!” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says his men will fight. He gives Jack a flat wooden box and tells them to ride to the sand hills as fast as they can and protect the box with their lives.

paragraphs.context: Jack frantically tried to stuff the box into his shoulder bag.
paragraphs.simple: Before Jack can put the box in his bag, Mamoon hits his camel and she runs. Jack drops the reins. He holds the saddle with one hand and the box with the other.

paragraphs.context: Annie’s camel ran beside Jack’s.
paragraphs.simple: The two camels run like racehorses. Jack rocks wildly and begs Beauty to slow down.

paragraphs.context: It was no use. Beauty ran like the wind.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The camels fly over the sand.
paragraphs.simple: Beauty does not slow down. Jack wants her to stop, but he also wants to get away from the bandits.

paragraphs.context: Finally the camels began to slow their pace.
paragraphs.simple: At last the camels slow down. No one is following them.

paragraphs.context: When the two camels reached the dunes
paragraphs.simple: The camels walk around the steep sand hills and stop between tall piles of sand.

paragraphs.context: “I hope Mamoon and the others are safe from the bandits,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack hopes Mamoon is safe. Annie asks what is in the box.

paragraphs.context: Jack held up the flat wooden box.
paragraphs.simple: Jack does not know, but Mamoon said to protect it with their lives.

paragraphs.context: “I hope it’s more than that,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack would not like to risk his life for spices.

paragraphs.context: “But don’t you think we could protect it better
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they could protect it better if they knew what it was. Jack agrees.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried to open the lid of the box, but he couldn’t.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels a keyhole. The box is locked.

paragraphs.context: Jack listened. He heard a high-pitched moaning sound.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears a high sad sound, like a violin, moving through the sand hills.

paragraphs.context: Jack held his breath.
paragraphs.simple: Jack hears horses running across the desert. He thinks it is the bandits.

paragraphs.context: “In the sand!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie makes her camel kneel. They jump off and start digging.

paragraphs.context: The sound of hoofbeats grew louder and louder.
paragraphs.simple: The horses get louder. They dig fast, like puppies.

paragraphs.context: “That’s deep enough!” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts the box in the hole and they cover it with sand.

paragraphs.context: A dark figure on a camel was silhouetted
paragraphs.simple: A dark rider on a camel comes toward them through the sand hills. Jack's heart beats very hard.

paragraphs.context: The rider drew closer, until he stopped
paragraphs.simple: The rider stops and asks if they are safe. It is Mamoon!

paragraphs.context: Relief flooded through Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels great relief and laughs.

paragraphs.context: “My men fought well,” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon's men fought well. The thieves ran away with only a few bags of pepper and beads.

paragraphs.context: “And we kept your box safe, too!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie proudly digs up the box and gives it to Mamoon.

paragraphs.context: “A priceless treasure,” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says the box holds a treasure he brought from Greece to Baghdad. He thanks them for guarding it.

paragraphs.context: “Sure, no problem,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack still wonders what is in the box: gold, silver, jewels?

paragraphs.context: But Mamoon did not say.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon does not tell. He puts the box in his bag and says they should go.

paragraphs.context: Jack climbed on top of his kneeling camel.
paragraphs.simple: Jack clucks his tongue and Beauty stands up. He is pleased.

paragraphs.context: “We will catch up with the others in Baghdad,”
paragraphs.simple: They will meet the others in Baghdad. If all goes well, they will get there in the afternoon. They must go east, toward the morning sun.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon rode out of the dunes.
paragraphs.simple: They ride out of the sand hills. Daylight shines over the sand.

paragraphs.context: “Ah, yes,” said Mamoon, “the whistling sands.”
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says the music they heard was "the whistling sands".

background.note: "Singing" or "whistling" sand dunes are real. When sand slides down a dune, it can make a deep humming or moaning sound.

paragraphs.context: “Some say it is magic,” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon thinks everything in nature has a reason. Science means watching the world and doing experiments to find out why things happen. The sound comes from sand moving down the sand hills.

background.note: In Baghdad's golden age, scholars did experiments and careful study in medicine, astronomy, math and chemistry. Their work helped later science in Europe.

paragraphs.context: “Learning the reasons for things is magic,” said Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says learning why things happen is a kind of magic. True knowledge brings light to the world.

paragraphs.context: Swaying from side to side on their camels
paragraphs.simple: They ride toward the sunrise. The desert becomes very hot. A dry wind makes snake-like lines in the sand.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon halted his camel. He looked around and frowned.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon stops and frowns.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon shook his head. “No, it is the desert itself
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon is not worried about bandits now. He is worried about the desert. It is "restless".

paragraphs.context: As they rode over the restless desert, the wind picked up loose sand
paragraphs.simple: The wind throws sand into the air. They keep their heads down. Their head cloths fly in the wind. The desert seems alive.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon stopped again and looked about.
paragraphs.simple: The lines in the sand become circles. Jack hears a moaning sound and hopes it is the whistling sands.

paragraphs.context: “No,” said Mamoon. “That is the cry of a terrible sandstorm.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says it is the sound of a terrible sandstorm, and it will be here soon.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, a haze of sand was spreading over the desert.
paragraphs.simple: Far away, sand spreads over the desert. The sky turns red, and the sand becomes a brown cloud that moves toward them like a wall.

paragraphs.context: “Get down! Lie on your bellies!” ordered Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon tells them to lie down on their stomachs and cover their faces with their head cloths.

paragraphs.context: Jack clucked his tongue. Beauty knelt to the ground.
paragraphs.simple: The camels kneel. Jack, Annie and Mamoon get off and lie on the sand next to them.

paragraphs.context: Jack tried desperately to cover his face with his head cloth
paragraphs.simple: The wind keeps pulling Jack's cloth away. The sky turns black, and the moaning becomes a loud roar.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up and saw the wind rip the saddlebag
paragraphs.simple: The wind tears the bag off Mamoon's camel. The box falls out and rolls away.

paragraphs.context: “The treasure!” cried Jack, but his voice was drowned out by the wind.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shouts, but no one can hear him. He runs after the box.

paragraphs.context: Jack raced across the desert as the sand battered his body.
paragraphs.simple: Sand hits Jack and the wind pushes him, but he runs as hard as he can. He catches the box, falls on top of it and covers his face.

paragraphs.context: The sandstorm blasted over Jack
paragraphs.simple: The storm roars like a hundred running camels. Jack's eyes burn, and he can hardly breathe.

paragraphs.context: Slowly the thundering softened to a low rumbling.
paragraphs.simple: Slowly the noise gets quieter. The wind stops. The desert is still and silent.

paragraphs.context: Coughing, Jack rolled over and sat up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack has sand in his mouth, ears and nose. He rubs his eyes, but that makes them worse.

paragraphs.context: Blinking, Jack clutched the box and looked around for the others.
paragraphs.simple: The air is full of dust. Jack does not know which way is which.

paragraphs.context: Jack clutched the small wooden box and stood up.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's legs are so weak that he falls. He calls Annie in a rough voice.

paragraphs.context: “There you are!” said Annie, stumbling out of the haze.
paragraphs.simple: Annie comes out of the dust. They are both okay.

paragraphs.context: “I had to save the box,” said Jack. “Where’s Mamoon?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack asks where Mamoon is. Annie does not know; he did not see them run after the box.

paragraphs.context: Peering through the sandy haze, Jack heard thumping sounds.
paragraphs.simple: Their two camels come running to them.

paragraphs.context: “He must have gone in the wrong direction to look for us,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Mamoon went the wrong way to look for them.

paragraphs.context: “If we don’t find him, how will we get to Baghdad?
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks how they will get to Baghdad and what to do with the treasure.

paragraphs.context: “Look, the top’s broken,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: There is a long crack in the lid of the box.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. He still thought Mamoon might not want them
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Mamoon might not want them to look, but he wants to know too much. They will just check that the treasure is okay.

paragraphs.context: Jack pried apart the two pieces of wood and lifted them off.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opens the broken box. Inside is a book.

paragraphs.context: “A book?” said Jack, surprised.
paragraphs.simple: Jack expected gold. The book has a plain leather cover with no title.

paragraphs.context: “Maybe the writing inside is the treasure,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The words may be the treasure.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks the writing inside may be the treasure.

paragraphs.context: Jack gently opened the book.
paragraphs.simple: The book has thick yellow pages sewn together, with writing on both sides. The first page says "The Writings of Aristotle".

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know,” said Jack. “I’ll look him up in our research book.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack cleans the sand off the research book and finds Aristotle in the index.

paragraphs.context: Aristotle (say AIR-is-TAH-tul) lived in ancient Greece
paragraphs.simple: Aristotle lived in Greece more than 2,300 years ago. He was one of the greatest philosophers ever. "Philosopher" means "lover of wisdom". Arabs brought his books to Europe in the Middle Ages.

background.note: Aristotle (384-322 BC) was a Greek thinker who wrote about science, nature, logic and how to live well. Scholars in Baghdad translated his books into Arabic.
The Middle Ages were the time in Europe from about the year 500 to 1500.

paragraphs.context: “I guess so,” said Jack. “But I wonder why this book is such a treasure.”
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders why the book is so valuable.

paragraphs.context: “Wait a minute,” said Annie. “Doesn’t Merlin’s note tell us
paragraphs.simple: Annie remembers: they must help the caliph spread wisdom to the world.

paragraphs.context: Jack caught his breath.
paragraphs.simple: Jack understands: the book is full of wisdom, and they must take it to the caliph. That is their mission!

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie pulled on the reins of their camels
paragraphs.simple: They get on the camels, leave the broken box and pack the book carefully in Jack's bag.

paragraphs.context: “Toward the rising sun in the east,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack remembers Mamoon said to go east, toward the rising sun.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie’s camels headed into the dusty, glaring sun.
paragraphs.simple: They ride into the bright sun. Annie says they are doing Merlin's second instruction: "Ride through the dust and hot morning light."

paragraphs.context: As Jack and Annie kept traveling toward the east
paragraphs.simple: The sand shines with heat. The air is clear, but they cannot see Mamoon.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked down to shield his eyes from the burning sunlight.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is very tired and falls asleep on the swaying camel. Annie shouts.

paragraphs.context: In the distance, Jack saw sunlit towers and domes
paragraphs.simple: Far away Jack sees towers and domes shining in the sun. It is Baghdad!

paragraphs.context: As Beauty and Cutie walked toward Baghdad
paragraphs.simple: Near Baghdad the sand becomes hard ground, then grass. Goats and sheep eat grass, and there are farms.

paragraphs.context: It wasn’t long before Jack and Annie came to a red clay path.
paragraphs.simple: Soon they reach a crossroads where travelers come from all directions to the city: boys with sheep, farmers in donkey carts and women with veils carrying pots.

paragraphs.context: Jack kept looking for Mamoon.
paragraphs.simple: Jack cannot see Mamoon. The camels cross a bridge over a yellow-brown river with boats on it.

background.note: Baghdad was built on the Tigris River. The Tigris and the Euphrates are the two great rivers of Iraq.

paragraphs.context: On the other side of the river was a huge outdoor market
paragraphs.simple: Across the river is a huge market with many tents and people from many countries. It smells of incense. Shoemakers, potters and weavers are working.

paragraphs.context: “Paper? Pearls?” a merchant shouted.
paragraphs.simple: Sellers shout to Jack and Annie, but they say no thanks.

paragraphs.context: In the ninth century, traders from all over the world
paragraphs.simple: In the 800s, traders from Spain, India, Africa, China, Greece and other lands came to sell things in Baghdad. Baghdad sold paper, fine cloth and jewelry. The big outdoor market is called a bazaar.

background.note: A bazaar is a market with many small shops or stalls, especially in the Middle East.
People in Baghdad learned to make paper from the Chinese around the year 800. Paper made books cheaper, so learning spread fast.

paragraphs.context: “Oh, so a bazaar is sort of like a mall,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says a bazaar is like a shopping mall. Annie says it is much better and wants to look around.

paragraphs.context: “We don’t have time to shop,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must finish the mission. He reads Merlin's letter again.

paragraphs.context: “It sounds like we pass three walls and then we come to a horse,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks they must pass three walls and then they will find a horse.

paragraphs.context: Jack put the book and letter away.
paragraphs.simple: They ride out of the market and come to a curved brick wall with a muddy moat (a ditch of water) at the bottom.

background.note: Caliph al-Mansur built Baghdad in 762 as a "Round City", with curved (round) walls one inside another and the caliph's palace and the green dome in the center.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie rode the two camels over an arched bridge
paragraphs.simple: They cross a bridge over the moat and go through a gate with iron doors. Inside is a busy street with buildings.

paragraphs.context: During its golden age, Baghdad had good hospitals.
paragraphs.simple: In its golden age, Baghdad had good hospitals, good police, public schools, many libraries and stores, and a zoo with a hundred lions.

paragraphs.context: Their camels clopped down the busy avenue
paragraphs.simple: They come to a green field and a second wall.

paragraphs.context: Bordering the field was another wall.
paragraphs.simple: The second wall is much taller, maybe a hundred feet (30 meters) high. There are guards, but they do not stop anyone.

paragraphs.context: “Act normal,” Jack advised Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie to act normally so the guards will not notice them.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie joined a stream of people passing through the gate.
paragraphs.simple: They pass the gate with other people. After another wide street they see the third wall.

paragraphs.context: The third wall was even taller than the second.
paragraphs.simple: The third wall is even taller, but people walk through freely. Annie thinks this part is easy.

paragraphs.context: “Yeah,” said Jack. “But we still have to find that horse on the dome
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they still must find the horse, find the caliph and get him to meet them.

paragraphs.context: Beauty and Cutie ambled through the gate of the third wall
paragraphs.simple: In the center of Baghdad is a palace with a shining green dome. On top of the dome is a statue of a horse.

background.note: The caliph's palace in the Round City had a famous green dome. Old stories say a statue of a horse rider stood on top of it.

paragraphs.context: “Yay, the horse who sees all!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie thinks the caliph lives in the palace. They follow people through an arch.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie rode under the arch and into a beautiful garden.
paragraphs.simple: They ride into a garden that smells of flowers. Boys are playing ball in a courtyard, and there is a stable with camels.

paragraphs.context: “Looks like we’ll have to go the rest of the way on foot,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they must walk from here. The camels can stay in the stable.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie rode into the stable.
paragraphs.simple: In the stable, the camels kneel. A ball rolls in, and Annie takes it outside.

paragraphs.context: “Here!” shouted a young boy with curly black hair.
paragraphs.simple: A curly-haired boy catches Annie's good throw and asks who they are.

paragraphs.context: “Our caliph is the most powerful man in the world,” said another boy.
paragraphs.simple: The boys laugh: the caliph has no time for children.

paragraphs.context: “That’s what everyone keeps saying,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie starts to say they have an important mission.

paragraphs.context: “Annie,” Jack interrupted, “come on.
paragraphs.simple: Jack stops Annie. He says his bag is in the stable, and they should go.

paragraphs.context: “When you discover that the caliph will not meet with you
paragraphs.simple: The boy says to come back and play when the caliph says no.

paragraphs.context: Annie stopped. “Don’t worry,” she called back.
paragraphs.simple: Annie shouts that the caliph will meet them because they are special.

paragraphs.context: “For one thing, we just saved a precious treasure
paragraphs.simple: Annie starts to tell about saving the treasure from bandits and a sandstorm.

paragraphs.context: “Annie!” Jack said sternly.
paragraphs.simple: Jack takes Annie's arm and pulls her away.

paragraphs.context: As they headed back into the stable, Jack shook his head.
paragraphs.simple: Jack tells Annie not to say things like that.

paragraphs.context: “Because it’s bragging,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says bragging makes other kids feel bad, even if you are special.

paragraphs.context: Jack’s leather bag lay at Beauty’s feet.
paragraphs.simple: Jack's bag is open. The cover of Aristotle's book is torn, and Beauty is happily chewing the wet pages of the treasure!

paragraphs.context: Jack ran to Beauty and yanked hunks of paper from her mouth.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They try to save the pages.
paragraphs.simple: Jack pulls paper out of Beauty's mouth. Annie picks up the torn pieces from the floor.

paragraphs.context: Jack was stunned. “I shouldn’t have left my bag here,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack is shocked. He says he should not have left his bag there.

paragraphs.context: “No, it’s all my fault.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says it is her fault, because she went back and bragged.

paragraphs.context: “I should have acted more humble, like Merlin said.”
paragraphs.simple: Annie says she should have been humble, as Merlin said. She almost cries.

paragraphs.context: “It’s okay,” said Jack. But he knew it wasn’t.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it is okay, but he knows the book is destroyed and they have failed.

paragraphs.context: Jack shook his head. “No, we can’t,” he said.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says the book is completely destroyed and cannot be fixed.

paragraphs.context: Annie looked up. “What—what did you just say?”
paragraphs.simple: Annie suddenly notices Jack's words.

paragraphs.context: A big grin crossed Annie’s face.
paragraphs.simple: Annie smiles: "It can't be fixed!" She asks Jack to help collect all the pieces.

paragraphs.context: “Why?” said Jack. Had Annie gone nuts?
paragraphs.simple: Jack thinks Annie has gone crazy.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie rushed around the stable, gathering up all the torn pages.
paragraphs.simple: They hurry and pick up every torn page.

paragraphs.context: “Now pile everything over here on top of the cover
paragraphs.simple: Annie asks for the book. Jack does not understand at first, then takes out the rhyme book.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened the book and read down the list.
paragraphs.simple: Jack finds "Mend What Cannot Be Mended".

paragraphs.context: Jack flipped through the pages until he came to the rhyme.
paragraphs.simple: Standing in a beam of sunlight, Jack reads his line loudly.

paragraphs.context: Heal what is broken beyond repair!
paragraphs.simple: "Make whole what is too broken to fix!"

paragraphs.context: The paper bits fluttered.
paragraphs.simple: The bits of paper fly up and spin like a small tornado. The spinning pulls the pieces together and becomes a bright light.

paragraphs.context: Jack shielded his eyes. He heard a loud whoof!
paragraphs.simple: Jack covers his eyes. With a loud noise, the bright tornado disappears.

paragraphs.context: Lying on the floor of the stable in front of Jack and Annie was the ancient book.
paragraphs.simple: The old book lies on the floor.

paragraphs.context: Holding his breath, Jack carefully picked up the treasure.
paragraphs.simple: Jack opens it. Aristotle's words are on the pages, with no tear anywhere.

paragraphs.context: “Thank goodness,” breathed Annie.
paragraphs.simple: Annie is very glad.

paragraphs.context: “I don’t know,” said Jack. “What’s the next thing Merlin tells us to do?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack reads Merlin's letter again.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly Jack heard someone behind them.
paragraphs.simple: A girl in a long white dress is at the door. A veil hides her hair and face.

paragraphs.context: “I am a servant of the palace,” the girl whispered.
paragraphs.simple: The girl whispers that she is a palace servant and asks them to follow.

paragraphs.context: “Where is she taking us?” asked Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wonders where she is taking them and why she whispers. Annie feels they should follow.

paragraphs.context: “Okay,” said Jack. He put the book of wisdom
paragraphs.simple: Jack puts both books in his bag and follows.

paragraphs.context: The three of them walked through the courtyard and through the palace doors.
paragraphs.simple: They walk down a wide hallway with candles and a thick carpet.

paragraphs.context: At the end of the hallway was a tall, carved door.
paragraphs.simple: A boy servant stands by a tall door. His face is almost hidden by his head cloth.

paragraphs.context: The servant girl stood close to Jack and Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The girl says: bow to the floor in front of the chair; do not look up or speak until someone speaks to you.

paragraphs.context: The boy servant pulled open the heavy door.
paragraphs.simple: The boy opens the door, the girl pushes them in, and the door closes.

paragraphs.context: “Jack, look! We’re here!” said Annie. “The Room of the Tree!”
paragraphs.simple: Annie sees that this is the Room of the Tree.

paragraphs.context: Jack turned around. A giant tree stood in the center of the room.
paragraphs.simple: In the middle of the room is a big tree with silver leaves. Golden machine birds sing on its branches.

background.note: Old writers tell of a real tree of silver and gold in a caliph's palace in Baghdad, with metal birds that moved and sang. It was made to amaze visitors.

paragraphs.context: Beneath the strange tree was an empty black chair.
paragraphs.simple: Under the tree is an empty black chair with jewels.

paragraphs.context: “Not really,” said Jack. “Where are the two friends?”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they have not met the two friends yet.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie knelt in front of the shiny black chair.
paragraphs.simple: They kneel and bow to the floor. Jack holds his bag tightly.

paragraphs.context: “But there’s no one here,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack feels silly bowing to an empty chair.

paragraphs.context: The door opened with a low creaking sound.
paragraphs.simple: The door opens. Jack shuts his eyes and hears footsteps.

paragraphs.context: “How did you get into the throne room?”
paragraphs.simple: A deep, rough voice asks how they got in.

paragraphs.context: “We have a priceless treasure to give to the caliph of Baghdad,”
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they have a book of wisdom for the caliph.

paragraphs.context: Jack fumbled in his bag and pulled out the book.
paragraphs.simple: With his eyes closed, Jack holds the book up.

paragraphs.context: “How did you come to be in possession of this book?”
paragraphs.simple: The man asks how they got the book.

paragraphs.context: “We were helping a friend,” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: They were helping a friend and lost him in a sandstorm.

paragraphs.context: “Ah, then I suppose you brought this book to Baghdad to gain a reward,”
paragraphs.simple: The man thinks they want a reward.

paragraphs.context: “No! No, we didn’t,” said Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says it was their mission to give it to the caliph.

paragraphs.context: “Surely you must be seeking some payment in exchange for this treasure,”
paragraphs.simple: The man offers sweet perfumes, but Annie says no.

paragraphs.context: “Rubies as large as hens’ eggs?” said the man.
paragraphs.simple: He offers rubies as big as eggs. Jack says no.

paragraphs.context: “You would not accept the book’s weight in gold?”
paragraphs.simple: He offers gold. Jack says they do not need a reward.

paragraphs.context: “Since he likes books so much, why don’t you just tell the caliph
paragraphs.simple: Annie says the caliph should use his gold and rubies to buy more books.

paragraphs.context: Again, there was silence. Then the man cleared his throat.
paragraphs.simple: The man's voice is now gentle and sounds familiar. He tells them to look up.

paragraphs.context: Jack opened his eyes. He slowly lifted his head.
paragraphs.simple: Jack sees gold slippers, a white robe with gold trim, and a face he knows.

paragraphs.context: Jack gasped. He couldn’t believe his eyes.
paragraphs.simple: Jack is amazed: the man is Mamoon!

paragraphs.context: “Yes,” said Mamoon. “I am very glad to see that you have safely arrived
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon is glad they arrived safely. Annie says they were worried about him.

paragraphs.context: “I looked everywhere for you after the sandstorm,”
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon looked everywhere, then sadly went back to Baghdad. He asks if they found their family.

paragraphs.context: “And we found your book,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They give the book to the caliph.
paragraphs.simple: Jack says they decided to give the book to the caliph.

paragraphs.context: Mamoon smiled. “You still do not understand, do you?”
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon smiles: they still do not understand.

paragraphs.context: “I am Caliph Abdullah al-Mamoon.”
paragraphs.simple: Mamoon says he is Caliph Abdullah al-Mamoon.

background.note: Abdullah al-Mamoon (al-Ma'mun, 786-833) was caliph from 813 to 833. He supported scholars and helped make the House of Wisdom famous.

paragraphs.context: “For many years, I have wanted a book of Aristotle’s wisdom,”
paragraphs.simple: The caliph wanted a book of Aristotle for many years. He heard one was found in Damascus and bought it. He wanted to travel in the desert again, as when he was a boy, so he dressed as a simple merchant. His men did not know who he really was.

paragraphs.context: “You have shown me that you have a great respect for books and learning,”
paragraphs.simple: The caliph says they respect books and learning, and they have humble hearts. He wants to show them a special place: the House of Wisdom.

paragraphs.context: “It is my hope that the world will indeed find it ‘great,’”
paragraphs.simple: The caliph hopes the world will find it great. He leaves the room and they follow.

paragraphs.context: Carrying the ancient book of Aristotle, the caliph led Jack and Annie
paragraphs.simple: The caliph walks quickly down the hall in his gold-trimmed robe. Everyone he passes bows to the floor.

paragraphs.context: “Another mystery solved!” Annie said to Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Annie says they have solved another part of the letter.

paragraphs.context: “Both friends are the same person!” said Annie.
paragraphs.simple: The old friend (Mamoon from the desert) and the new friend (the caliph) are the same person!

paragraphs.context: The caliph led Jack and Annie out the front doors of the palace.

parts.text: He believes knowledge cannot belong to only one person or country.
parts.meaning: He thinks knowledge is not for one person or country.

parts.text: It belongs to all.
parts.meaning: It is for everyone.

sentences.grammar: "Belong to" means be owned by. "All" here means all people.

sentences.context: The world grows wise only when wisdom is shared.
sentences.simple: The world becomes wise only if people share what they know.

parts.text: The world grows wise
parts.meaning: The world becomes wise

parts.text: only when wisdom is shared.
parts.meaning: only if people share wisdom.

sentences.grammar: "Grow + adjective" means become. "Is shared" is passive: people share wisdom.

sentences.context: It seems someone from our land has traveled to yours and shared our stories.
sentences.simple: It looks like a person from our country went to your country and told our stories there.

parts.text: It seems
parts.job: How the caliph knows: it looks true.
parts.meaning: It looks like

parts.text: someone from our land has traveled to yours
parts.meaning: a person from our country went to your country

parts.text: and shared our stories.
parts.meaning: and told our stories.

sentences.grammar: "Yours" means your land. "Has traveled ... and (has) shared" uses the present perfect.

act normal.meaning: To behave in the usual way, so no one notices you.
act normal.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at a loss for words.meaning: So surprised or shy that you do not know what to say.
at a loss for words.example: Even Annie seemed to be at a loss for words
at a loss for words.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

at the same time.example: But at the same time, he wanted to get far away from the bandits.
at the same time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

attract attention.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

be full of.meaning: To have a lot of something.
be full of.example: it must be full of wisdom
be full of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

be upon someone.meaning: To come to someone, very soon. "Night will soon be upon us" means it will soon be night.
be upon someone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

break in.meaning: To start talking while another person is talking; to interrupt.
break in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by mistake.meaning: Not on purpose; because of an error.
by mistake.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

by the time.example: By the time they had filled their baskets
by the time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

by the way.meaning: You say "by the way" to start talking about something new.
by the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

can't believe your eyes.meaning: To be very surprised by what you see.
can't believe your eyes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

carry on.example: He carried on his father’s work
carry on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up with.meaning: To reach someone who is ahead of you.
catch up with.example: We will catch up with the others in Baghdad,
catch up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment because you are suddenly surprised or excited.
catch your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

chase after.meaning: To run after someone or something to catch them.
chase after.example: I don’t think he saw us chase after the box.
chase after.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

cluck your tongue.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

die down.example: Then the wind died down as quickly as it had started.
die down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

draw close.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

drown out.meaning: A loud sound "drowns out" another sound when it is so loud that you cannot hear the other one.
drown out.example: his voice was drowned out by the wind.
drown out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

easy for you to say.meaning: You say this when something is easy for the other person but hard for you.
easy for you to say.example: “Easy for you to say,” said Jack.
easy for you to say.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fight off.meaning: To fight someone so that they go away.
fight off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

find out.meaning: To learn something that you did not know.
find out.example: “We’ll find out when we get there,”
find out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

find your way.meaning: To find the right way to a place.
find your way.example: We need to find our way.
find your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for one thing.meaning: You say this to give the first reason. "For another" gives the next reason.
for one thing.example: For one thing, we just saved a precious treasure
for one thing.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for the hundredth time.meaning: Again, after doing it many, many times before.
for the hundredth time.example: For the hundredth time, he stared at the title on the cover:
for the hundredth time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

from side to side.meaning: Moving to the left and then to the right, again and again.
from side to side.example: As the camels swung from side to side
from side to side.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

gather up.meaning: To pick up and collect things that are spread out.
gather up.example: Help me gather up all these pieces!
gather up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get going.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get the best of.meaning: "His curiosity got the best of him" means he wanted to know so much that he could not stop himself.
get the best of.example: But his curiosity got the best of him.
get the best of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give someone a look.meaning: To look at someone in a way that shows what you think (here: "No!").
give someone a look.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

give up.example: Finally I gave up my search
give up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

go nuts.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

grab hold of.meaning: To take something suddenly and hold it tightly.
grab hold of.example: He grabbed hold of the nearest tree trunk.
grab hold of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold your breath.meaning: To stop breathing for a moment, because you are excited, afraid or waiting.
hold your breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

if all goes well.example: If all goes well, we will arrive in the city in the afternoon.
if all goes well.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in and out of.meaning: Going into a place and out again, many times; between things.
in and out of.example: As their camels wove slowly in and out of the crowd
in and out of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in exchange for.meaning: Given to pay for something else.
in exchange for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in possession of.meaning: Having or owning something. "Come to be in possession of" means come to have.
in possession of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the distance.example: In the distance were lonely dunes.
in the distance.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in the lead.meaning: At the front, first in a line or group.
in the lead.example: The man in the lead made his camel kneel.
in the lead.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

join in.meaning: To start doing something with other people.
join in.example: The other camel riders joined in.
join in.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep an eye out for.meaning: To watch carefully for someone or something.
keep an eye out for.example: keep an eye out for a big boat.
keep an eye out for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

keep going.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep out.meaning: To stop something from coming in.
keep out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

lay the foundation for.meaning: To build the first, most important part that other things are later built on.
lay the foundation for.example: helped lay the foundation for modern science.
lay the foundation for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let go.meaning: To stop holding something. "Let go of" means stop holding.
let go.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

like the wind.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

load down.meaning: To give a person or an animal a lot of heavy things to carry. "Loaded down with" means carrying a lot of.
load down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

long for.meaning: To want something very much. "Long to be" means want very much to be.
long for.example: I always longed for more blankets
long for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

look up.meaning: 1. To raise your eyes and look up ("Jack looked up"). 2. To look for a word or fact in a book ("I'll look it up").
look up.example: Jack and Annie looked up at the open window.
look up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

lose your way.example: Sandstorms can easily cause travelers to lose their way in the desert.
lose your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make a joke.example: as if they thought Annie was making a joke.
make a joke.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make it.meaning: To succeed in getting to a place. (Different: "making it hard to see" = causing it to be hard to see.)
make it.example: I can’t believe we made it all the way here.
make it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

no problem.meaning: "I can easily do it" or "It is all right."
no problem.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no use.meaning: "It is no use" means it will not help.
no use.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

not at all.example: He did not feel at all safe
not at all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

nothing but.example: there was nothing but sand and sky.
nothing but.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

of all time.example: one of the greatest philosophers of all time.
of all time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

oh, brother.meaning: What you say when you feel a little tired of something or a little annoyed. It is not about a real brother.

oh, man.meaning: What you say when you feel strongly: surprised, afraid, tired or happy. It is like "Oh, wow!" or "Oh, no!" It is not about a man.

on foot.example: Looks like we’ll have to go the rest of the way on foot,
on foot.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

on your way.meaning: Traveling to a place. "Let us be on our way" means let us leave and go now.
on your way.example: It brought them here on their way to Baghdad!
on your way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

one thing at a time.meaning: Doing things one after another, not all together.
one thing at a time.example: we have to do things in order, one thing at a time.
one thing at a time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of nowhere.meaning: Suddenly, from no place you can see.
out of nowhere.example: Make Helpers Appear out of Nowhere.
out of nowhere.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of the way.meaning: Moving to a place where you will not be hit or be in the way.
out of the way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

over time.example: But over time, I have come to love the cold desert nights,
over time.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pick up.meaning: 1. To lift something up or take it in your hand ("She picked up a folded letter"). 2. (Of wind) to become stronger ("As the wind picked up").
pick up.example: As the wind picked up, the sky turned red
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pull on.meaning: 1. To put on clothes quickly ("He pulled on his jacket"). 2. To pull something toward you ("pulled on the reins").
pull on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put aside.meaning: To put something to one side because you are not using it now.
put aside.example: Jack put his math homework aside.
put aside.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put it that way.meaning: "When you put it that way" means "When you say it like that (I agree)."
put it that way.example: “I guess, when you put it that way,”
put it that way.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

put out.example: The camel riders put out their small fire.
put out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

risk your life.meaning: To do something dangerous where you might die.
risk your life.example: I’d hate to risk my life for cinnamon or pepper.
risk your life.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

saddle up.meaning: To put a saddle on a horse or camel, to get ready to ride.
saddle up.example: helped them saddle up their animals
saddle up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

send for.example: I hope Merlin sends for us again soon.
send for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sense of direction.meaning: Knowing which way is north, south and so on, or which way to go.
sense of direction.example: He had completely lost his sense of direction.
sense of direction.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

set sail.meaning: To start a trip by ship. Mamoon jokes that they will "set sail" on camels.
set sail.example: We will set sail on them soon.
set sail.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shade your eyes.meaning: To hold your hand over your eyes to keep the bright light out.
shade your eyes.example: Shading their eyes from the bright sunlight
shade your eyes.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

shake your head.meaning: To move your head from side to side to say "no" or to show you are unhappy.
shake your head.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

ship of the desert.meaning: A camel. People call camels "ships of the desert" because they carry people and goods across the desert, and they rock like ships.
ship of the desert.example: We love our ships of the desert, too,
ship of the desert.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

slow down.meaning: To become slower; to go less fast.
slow down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

sort of.meaning: A little; in some way. (Friendly talk.)
sort of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

sound out.meaning: To say a new word slowly, one part at a time.
sound out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

such as.example: precious spices, such as cinnamon, pepper, and vanilla.
such as.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

table of contents.meaning: The list of chapters or parts at the front of a book.
table of contents.example: read down the table of contents together.
table of contents.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

take a deep breath.meaning: To breathe in a lot of air, often to make yourself calm.
take a deep breath.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

take off.meaning: 1. To leave or start running suddenly. 2. To take something off = to remove it ("taking saddlebags off the camels").
take off.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

thank goodness.meaning: You say this when you are very glad that something bad did not happen.
thank goodness.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

turn into.meaning: To change and become something different.
turn into.example: Jack’s backpack had turned into a leather shoulder bag.
turn into.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

watch out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

well suited to.meaning: Very right for something; having just what you need for it.
well suited to.example: She is well suited to travel in the desert,
well suited to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

with all your might.meaning: With all your strength; as hard as you can.
with all your might.example: Jack ran with all his might
with all your might.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

with your life.meaning: "Protect it with your lives" means protect it even if you die. "Hold on for your life" means hold on as hard as you can, because you are in danger.
with your life.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.
